utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Registrar, please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to resume work now. I wish to see whether the interpreters' booths are ready, our faithful interpreters. Very well, can everyone hear me, the Prosecution, the Defence, General Blaskic, my colleagues, can you hear me? Very well, in that case, we are ready. Mr. Prosecutor, it is up to you now to bring your witness. Let me look at our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours, good morning counsel. Mr. President and your Honours, the next witness we will call is Charles McLeod. Mr. McLeod will testify about a report which he prepared for ECMM in May 1993. First of all, let me give you some background about Mr. McLeod. Mr. McLeod was appointed to ECMM as a Monitor and spent a year as a member of the United Kingdom delegation to the ECMM which was based in Zagreb and that was in 1992. In December 1992, Mr. McLeod was sent to General Morrillon's headquarters in Kiseljak where he was an ECMM liaison officer between ECMM and UNPROFOR. Following the events in the Lasva Valley in April 1993, Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was head of the Regional Centre for ECMM in Zenica, and Ole Brix-Andersen, who was deputy head of mission, political section, sent Mr. McLeod to make an appraisal of what had occurred in the Lasva Valley in April 1993. Mr. McLeod then travelled to Zenica on 3rd May and remained in the area until 12th May, during which time he interviewed a variety of people, including various members of the parties, political, military and religious leaders. He also visited the villages of Ahmici and Loncari. He prepared a report on inter-ethnic violence in Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica in April 1993 on behalf of the ECMM humanitarian section. His report was then distributed to each of the member states of the European Community, amongst others. In July 1993, he joined the international conference on the former Yugoslavia as a political advisor and worked in that capacity to Mr. Stoltenberg's deputies, Ambassador Knut Vollebaek and Ambassador Kai Eide. We will present his report to your Honours and his testimony will concentrate on various aspects of that report and on interviews which he conducted, including interviews with Ivica Santic, Pero Skopljak, the accused Tihomir Blaskic, and Zlatko Aleksovski and others. Finally, Mr. President and your Honours, he will testify about his conclusions regarding the events in the Lasva Valley in April 1993. In respect of the indictment, your Honours, his testimony relates to virtually all counts contained in the indictment. That concludes my summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much. This report that you mentioned which he submitted, has it been communicated to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case all the conditions having been established for an adversarial debate. Please have Mr. McLeod brought in, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, we wish to preserve our hearsay objection as to apparently interviews of other individuals that this witness is going to be recounting wholesale. Obviously we are not going to have the opportunity to cross-examine those other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but the Chamber has made a ruling about hearsay, I wish to remind you. You cannot continue to insist on your objection, except if you wish it to enter the transcript, is it just a moral protest? If it only has a moral meaning, then it is all right. Thank you. Can you hear me, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please confirm your name and first name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Charles McLeod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: McLeod. Please read the solemn declaration that is being given to you by the usher, standing. MR. CHARLES McLEOD (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Tribunal thanks you for having accepted to come and appear in the trial against General Blaskic, who is here present. The Prosecutor has outlined the general framework of your testimony, and for an expert such as you, I will not reiterate what has already been said, so we are waiting for your testimony which will focus on the particular points underlined by the Prosecution in connection with the case against General Blaskic. Please feel free to present your testimony after which the Prosecutor will have some additional questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I am going to be asking you a number of questions in respect of your report on inter-ethnic violence in Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica in April 1993 and as I ask you these questions if you would pause after the conclusion of my question to give time for the interpreters to interpret my question before answering, otherwise my questions will merge with your answers and it will not be an effective presentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before turning to the substance of the report, Mr. McLeod, can you please tell the judges about your background and training, with particular emphasis on your training as a military officer and your experiences as a member of the ECMM in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I was born in London in 1963, and educated in England, and I joined the British army in 1982. I was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the infantry in 1983 and I served with my unit in Germany, I did a four month tour in west Belfast in Northern Ireland. While I was in the army, I then went to London University and read a Bachelor's degree in German for three years, and rejoined my unit in England, went back to Northern Ireland for a further two year tour, attended a junior command and staff course and my final job in the army was as adjutant of a training depot. As adjutant, amongst other things I was responsible for military discipline within the unit and I had experience of prosecuting at court's martial, prosecuting at about a dozen court's martial over a 18 month period. I left the army in 1992 and immediately joined the ECMM as a member of the UK delegation. With the ECMM, I was on two month contracts and completed a total of six contracts. Following my time with ECMM, I will come back and talk in some detail about what I was doing with ECMM in a moment, I spent a further year in the former Yugoslavia working for an international conference for the former Yugoslavia, working as political advisor to Mr. Stoltenberg's deputies, initially Ambassador Knut Volebaek and then Ambassador Kai Eide, and we were responsible for the negotiations which we were attempting to conduct between the Croatian government and the Serbs who occupied the Krajina region of Croatia at that time, so that was for a further year. At the end of that, I then did a Master's degree in business administration back in England, so turning with a bit more detail to what I was doing as a member of ECMM, initially I was a member of the Regional Centre in Zagreb, working as a Monitor, working on the separation of forces within Croatia on both sides of the internal contact line inside Croatia, so this is Serbs and Croats, and I was responsible for ensuring that troops had been withdrawn from the front-line and then that heavy weapons were being stored in the correct areas, and this meant liaising with military forces on both sides within Croatia. Fairly soon, I was then moved to the headquarters of the ECMM within the humanitarian section, and as a member of the humanitarian section, I was responsible for attempting to implement humanitarian policies such as there was. ECMM did not have great resources to carry out humanitarian works, but we did have teams deployed on the ground who observed things and who had information about humanitarian problems and issues, so one of the things I did was attempt to improve the information flow from our teams on the ground by then calculating a weekly humanitarian activity report, which we then disseminated to the international humanitarian agencies based in Zagreb, so they would have the benefit of the information we had from Croatia and Bosnia and this seemed to be fairly effective and well received. As a member of the humanitarian section, I was involved in ECMM's attempts to regain a position in northern Bosnia, Serb-controlled Bosnia, and so this took me on a couple of trips to Banja Luka, which was the headquarters of the Serb-controlled area in northern Bosnia. As a result of this, the ECMM was then approached by John Thompson, who was the head of what was then CSCE, Conference on Security and the Co-operation in Europe, a rapporteur mission which was sent to the camps of Manjaca and Trnopolje in northern Bosnia. Because ECMM had some limited access to Banja Luka, we were asked by John Thompson to take his rapporteur mission in, so I accompanied him to Manjaca and Trnopolje. Because of the liaison we had with the ICRC, we were then invited by the ICRC to accompany them as an international presence when they were removing detainees from these camps, which was an interesting experience. In Christmas 1992, I was at General Morrillon's headquarters in Kiseljak outside Sarajevo as the liaison officer for a four week period and during that time, I travelled from Kiseljak to Zenica and so saw what conditions were like on the road from Kiseljak through Busovaca to Zenica over the Christmas period in 1992. During March 1993, one of my key activities was attempting to, I think successfully, to set up a process of negotiation between the Croats and the Serbs in the Krajina to facilitate the collection of bodies who were stuck on the confrontation line near the Maslenica bridge in Croatia where there had been a fight in the January of that year. The fact there were dead bodies lying up in no-man's land was causing great concern, so with the headquarters, the Danish management of the ECMM established a programme and then negotiated with the Croats and the Serbs to facilitate the collection of these dead bodies and their repatriation across an UN controlled checkpoint which was I think of some benefit, because people were getting very concerned about this. Then in April of that year, the events which are all quite familiar took place in the Vitez area, and immediately after the events of 16th, 17th, 18th April, Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was a French Ambassador working for the ECMM as head of the region centre based in Zenica, came to Zagreb to the headquarters and met with Ole Brix-Andersen who was deputy head of the mission on the political side, so a Danish diplomat, to discuss the events, to discuss his concern about what was going on and he suggested that somebody should go and attempt to establish as clearly as possible what had actually taken place. He said that he could spare somebody to do this, but most of his teams were working flat out with bilateral meetings and trilateral meetings between the parties to try and stabilise the situation. At the same time, Thomas Osario, who was working for the UN Centre for Human Rights, also approached the headquarters of ECMM, said he was going down specifically to Ahmici to see what had gone on, and asked if somebody could go, so the decision was taken by the headquarters at ECMM that I, as somebody who had been working in the humanitarian section, should go to the Regional Centre in Zenica, very briefly try to establish what had gone on, and to come back and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that information. Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 242, Mr. Dubuisson, distributed to the various persons in the courtroom? Mr. President, Prosecutor's Exhibit 242 is a copy of Mr. McLeod's report on inter-ethnic violence in Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica in April 1993. There is an English and a French version of this report. Before turning our attention to that report, Mr. McLeod, let me ask you ultimately to whom was this report disseminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once the report was written, it was passed to the heads of each of the delegations of the ECMM, who then sent it on to their capitals, so each of the European Union capitals and various others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, can you inform the judges the dates that you actually went down to Central Bosnia to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I travelled into Zenica via Split on 3rd May and I left again on 12th May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In preparing your report, did you consult with ECMM monitors who were in the region and UNPROFOR personnel as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. When I arrived, my first action was to gather together all of the reports which had been written by ECMM and UNPROFOR and I sat down and spent a day or two days reading through all the reports and producing a digest of the events as they were reported, which is actually contained at the back of this report, plotted out all of the locations on the map so that I could build up a picture in my own mind of what we had seen, what the UN had seen, before I started talking to people so that I would have as clear an idea as possible, in advance, of what we thought had happened as a background against which I could then hear other people's versions of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the preparation of this report, did you travel on the ground to villages that had been essentially destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 4th May I travelled with Jean-Pierre Thebault, Ambassador Thebault, to visit the British battalion headquarters in Vitez and then accompanied Colonel Bob Stewart on a visit that he was making to the village of Ahmici, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also visit the village of Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, we went to Ahmici and then up to Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the course of preparing this report, Mr. McLeod, did you also interview political, military and religious leaders from the Muslim side and from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my objective had been as far as possible to get a balanced view and therefore to speak to the political -- in other words the mayors -- military commanders on both sides and also in order to be able to meet people who would be civic leaders on sides controlled by the opposition in each case, I met religious leaders because on both sides the religious leaders were the only people in territory controlled by the opposing parties whom I could find to build up as clear a view and as balanced a view as possible of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your report contains the interview statements of various persons whom you interviewed from the parties, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I wrote up detailed notes as I was actually meeting people and talking to people and then at the end of the period in Zenica and immediately on returning to Zagreb typed up those notes into the report and in almost every case attached them as an appendix to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you summarise, very briefly, the identities of the parties you interviewed? How many were there and who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I will do that by simply turning to the report and reading down the contents page, which is the second page in the report, and you can see there the dates of the meetings and who I was talking to. You can see that I met the mayor of Zenica, Father Stjepan, who was a Croatian priest, Catholic priest in Zenica; the head of the ICRC in Zenica, because I felt it was important to liaise with them as well; the commander of III Corps BiH in Zenica, so he was the Muslim military commander in the area and then the following day meeting with Father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a minute. It seems to me that in the French version I am missing the first two pages .

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Harmon. I have a report which begins with a statement of the mayor of Zenica and Vitez, so I suppose a report must start with an introduction, but I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, I was informed that this whole report had been translated into French and it was given to me and it appears the table of contents in the French version is not included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe what is important is the actual introduction, these two pages. Perhaps the witness in that introduction explains his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It appears, Mr. President, that your report, the French translation is not in the correct order. I do not see a table of contents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you direct Judge Jorda to where it is in the French translation? That would be helpful, Mr. McLeod. Apparently it is in there, apparently this has been assembled in the wrong order, Mr. President, I apologise. Mr. McLeod has found the index he is referring to and he can direct your Honour to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is better now. I have a schematic attitude, which may be a bit archaic, but this is much better now. I wish to thank the witness for helping me out. I apologise for not listening very carefully to your last answer, so could you please repeat it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, would you please then continue -- just start at the beginning of your answer, if you would. Identify please again the parties who you interviewed and whose reports are contained in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. As Mr. President can see on the table of contents, we have the dates down the left-hand side and then the details of the people that I met. You can see that I met with the mayor of Zenica, Father Stjepan, who was a Catholic priest, a Croat living in Zenica; the head of the ICRC mission in Zenica; the commander of III Corps of the BiH Army, so he was the senior Muslim military commander in the area, Father Bozo, who was another Croat Catholic priest in a village Cajdras just outside Zenica in an area controlled by the Muslims; the mayor of Vitez; General Blaskic, who was commander of the operational zone of Vitez, Colonel at that time; the deputy commander of the Kruscica brigade, which was a BiH Army brigade just outside Vitez; various members of BritBat. I actually noted the meeting I had with the second in command, Enver Hodza, who was the Imam of Busovaca, so clearly a Muslim living in Busovaca; the chief of police and a number of other policemen in Busovaca; the mayor of Zenica again; various people at the Centre for Human Rights in Zenica. I had a visit to Kaonik Prison which was the Croatian prison just outside Busovaca; a gentleman called Hasan Sadibasic who was a Muslim living in Vitez; and then finally another meeting with the deputy commander of III Corps of the BiH Army, a man named Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, before turning to the substance of those interviews, could you please explain your method of interviewing each of these people, what you did, what you said before the interview started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Because my aim had been to try and gather as clear a view as possible of what had happened, having initially armed myself with our own view of events as we had seen them and reported them, when I met each person, I explained to them that I had come from Zagreb, that the international community was extremely concerned about the events that had just taken place, that I had been sent here to meet everybody, to talk to them, that I was having this series of meetings balanced on both sides of the two parties, and I invited everybody to explain to me in their own words what they thought had happened. In order to facilitate this, I had a photocopied map of the area and a set of coloured pens and I would put the map in front of them and say "please show me on the map", which made life a lot easier, because otherwise they would talk about areas and places which would mean nothing to me, but when they pointed them out on the map, it was clear what they were talking about. As far as possible I tended not to contradict what they were saying when they were saying something I thought was wrong, but allow them to explain their point of view. My hope was that by hearing the points of view of the parties at different levels, the military, political and religious, at the end of it I would be able to build up a picture of what they thought had happened and then cross-reference that with what we had actually seen or what we believed had happened and that way, get as clear a view as possible of the events that had taken place. I also explained that our intention was to establish what had happened and then if possible work out ways of preventing it from happening again, but that was an ambition which at the time I think one would have admitted was slightly ambitious and probably was over ambitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by an interpreter and was another third party present with you during the conduct of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the normal policy of ECMM that we would work in two-man teams, almost exclusively two people of different nationalities and so for each of the meetings that I had here, I was accompanied either by Ambassador Thebault or by a Danish Monitor called Erik Friis-Pedersen, who was a member of the Regional Centre in Zenica. Again, because my linguistic ability in Serbo-Croat by the end of two years meant that I could understand conversations, at this point, about ten months into my tour, I was certainly not in a position to be able to have a conversation with anybody, so all of the meetings were held working through interpreters. For most of them, I was using an interpreter who was provided by the Regional Centre. For some of them, I was using interpreters provided by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I would like to focus your attention on certain of the interviews that are contained in your report. Let me start with the interview with Besim Spahic, who was mayor of Zenica. Could you please inform the judges about that particular interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. To help your Honours, this is summarised at annex A to the report, I am not quite sure where this will be in the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I am not sure for Judge Jorda's purposes whether or not this is in the right order, so Mr. President, do you have the interview before you of Mr. Spahic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I found it, thank you very much for your concern. This is the Exhibit 609.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please proceed then, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I met Mr. Spahic, who was the mayor of Zenica, on a couple of occasions, but he was initially the first person that I met in Zenica once I had started actually meeting the parties. I was accompanied by Erik Friis-Pedersen during the meeting. The mayor, Mr. Spahic, spoke for some time about the events and you can see the notes that I wrote as the interpreter spoke at the time and you can see certainly in the English version -- I am not sure my French is good enough to check the French version -- in the English version you can see the way the grammar moves slightly as the interpreter was speaking and I was simply scribbling notes as we went. He said basically that they had had this conflict, that the situation had deteriorated dramatically, that they had attempted to stabilise the situation within Zenica, he acknowledged that on the Muslim side in Zenica, various things had been done to the Croatian population and people had been arrested, people had been displaced, houses had been burnt, but what he was trying to stress was that they were attempting as far as possible to stabilise the situation, to get the Croatian population back to their houses where they had left their houses, and that where people were being victimised or had been evicted that the military and police -- the Muslim military and police formations were instructed to protect them, to provide local protection and that as far as possible, they were also trying to integrate the Croatian military formations who had been in Zenica anyway beforehand back into this "joint patrol", was the way it was described. So he quite clearly acknowledged that things had not been perfect, but that they were doing their very best to get back to some sort of normality. He said that on the other side, there was a lack of information about what was going on. He was particularly concerned about what was going on in Vitez, they knew that terrible things had happened in Ahmici because they had some refugees from Ahmici. During the conversation, he gave me a list of names of people that they understood had been arrested or were missing in Vitez. That list of names is attached as an annex to the report. In my copy of the French version, it occurs immediately afterwards as annex 2A. He gave me this piece of paper and said, "in your travels, McLeod, if you can find out anything about these people, we would be very grateful". He struck me as somebody who was trying to be fairly reasonable under very difficult circumstances and I think he acknowledged quite clearly that life was not perfect, but he was attempting to get to a stable integrated mixed, an ethnically mixed community. That seemed to be his aspiration, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, did he tell you what had happened to 2,000 Croats who had lived in south west Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that at the outbreak of hostilities, again on 16th April, a large proportion of the Croatian population had, for whatever reasons, decided they wanted to leave. I think that there had been a lot of propaganda -- I do not know if "propaganda" is the right word, there had been strong suggestions on the Croatian media from Vitez that these people ought to leave, so a lot of them had left their houses and moved across to Vitez. Some of them were now attempting to come back, but were being prevented from coming back to their houses, not by the Muslims, they were in Croatian-controlled territory and not able to get back to their houses in Zenica, so there had been quite a lot of displacement of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, who did he say was preventing the Croats who had been displaced from coming back into the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His understanding was that the Croats were not allowing these people to leave Croatian-controlled territory to come back into the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now you said, Mr. McLeod, that he was attempting to make sure that the population, the Croat population was safe in Zenica. Did he also give you copies of two decrees that were to the effect that those populations should be protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see -- I think we are going to have trouble finding them again in the French copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do not look for it, please continue with your statement. I will try and find it. In case I have a problem, I will tell you, but please go on with your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. We are looking for appendix 1 to the report, which is, "records for the return of refugees to Zenica". He gave me two documents, the first one dated 17th April, which is a decree on the establishment of the War Presidency of Zenica, and this document was basically saying that joint checkpoints -- in this case "joint" means joint Muslim and Croat within Zenica -- checkpoints and patrols should be set up to prevent atrocities being committed against minority population; that barricades which had been set up within the town preventing movement within the town should be taken down; investigation of crimes by the civil police; the provision of security by the civil police and the ABiH for all civilians within Zenica, both parts of the population; free access to hospitals; security of hospitals to be taken over by mixed civil police, mixed being Croat and Muslim; orders for a cease-fire and cessation of digging of trenches and filling in of trenches. Again, this is internally within Zenica, so on both sides, Muslim and Croat, within Zenica to stop digging trenches around their houses, and a Joint Commission consisting of the Civil Defence, the HVO, so the Croat military formation within Zenica, and ECMM, to go to the village Dobriljeno and stop the fighting. This is a reference to -- ECMM to a very large extent had tried to set up Joint Commissions where they would take military commanders from both sides, bring them together and share a meeting between them and get them to agree in a village if there was a problem, what the problem was and then get them to agree to stop, then the military commanders on both sides would persuade the local military commanders they had to stop whatever they were doing. This had been first tried in January of that year, when the conflict first started in Busovaca, and we were attempting to replicate the same thing, so this was a reference to a commission of that sort, to go to this village and stabilise the situation. The second document that he gave me, dated 18th April, again simply says that there should be an unconditional cease-fire and withdrawal of units from the contact line, and that the civil police and Civil Defence were obliged to provide security for people and property, and that conditions should be established for everybody who had left their houses to return to their houses, and that residents' committees should organise duty rosters, in other words security but without weapons, to ensure the security of houses and blocks of flats and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. McLeod, did the mayor give you a list of 13 men who were missing from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I mentioned earlier, he gave me this list of people. In my copy of the report what you can see at appendix 2 is the original list that he gave me and then a translation in English and -- yes, I then took that with me when I went to Vitez and spoke to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now turning to another set of interviews, Mr. McLeod, interviews with two Catholic priests who were Croats obviously, from the Zenica parish; can you tell the judges about those interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Here we started annex B to the report, which was a meeting I had with Father Stjepan. I believe he was the senior Catholic priest within Zenica, I met him in his house, accompanied by Ambassador Thebault. I again explained who I was, what I was doing there and asked him to tell me what, in his view, was going on. He was clearly a man who was working under a lot of pressure. He was very concerned about the welfare of his parishioners. He described the situation, as you can see in the report, listing in some detail things which had been done to the Croatian population in Zenica, the fact that some people had had their houses burnt, the fact some people had been robbed and some people killed, but overall what he was stressing was that there was an attempt being made with the authorities, this is the Muslim authorities, to engage with him to stabilise the situation, that his good offices were being used to try and bring back as far as possible a feeling of calm, that he had access to his parishioners, that he had some access to people who were in prison -- not complete access, this is one of the things which he raised with us; that quite a lot of people had left, this is Croats, had left Zenica, but that actually what people wanted to do now was to come back, the majority of them, to their houses, and this was being facilitated as far as possible. So he described a situation which was not pleasant, but where he gave the impression that the local authorities were doing their best under very difficult circumstances to return to the situation as it had been beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in fact did he not say that all of the authorities: "... all of them, except MOS, are doing their job very well and are very correct." That is on the third page, B3, top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, he was talking about the joint patrols and he said that in critical positions or critical situations, they needed to have these joint patrols because there was a risk of panic and he said that people did not trust the BiH, this is the army, or the MUP, who were the police, the civilian police. The note that I have of what he said is: "All I have to say is that all of them, except for MOS, are doing their job very well and are very correct." This is him sitting at his dining room table in his house in the middle of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, in your opinion, did Father Stjepan appear to you to be a moderate who advocated ethnic reconciliation not ethnic division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, he was under immense pressure, as one can imagine -- we cannot imagine, but he was under immense pressure, but he was trying as far as possible to allow his people, his parishioners to live in their houses and to, if possible, to return to the way they had been working before, which was an integrated ethnic city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you also turn your attention to the interview you had with Father Bozo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My note of the meeting with Father Bozo is at annex E to the report. Father Bozo was another Catholic priest in the village of Cajdras, which was south west of Zenica going up the road across the direct road from Zenica to Vitez. I met with him on the morning of 8th May, accompanied by Erik Friis-Pedersen. This meeting started off again with a meeting with him in his house, we then went on a tour of a village further up the road where a number of houses had been burnt and he wanted to show me this. We then returned back down to his house and the church and he stood on the steps of the church and a number of his parishioners, Croats -- it was a sort of public meeting and he read out a list of issues or complaints or concerns which he had. I believe that he was also of the team of Catholic priests working in the Zenica area, he was the priest who had responsible for visiting prisoners, so this is Croatian prisoners -- Croats being held in Muslim prisons. I think that because he was out on the edge of the town, closer to the confrontation line, the contact line, his perspective was slightly more extreme, because his parishioners had been exposed to more direct fighting up at the top of the contact line, on the high ground. He again felt that, and listed in detail, quite a lot of things had been done against his parishioners, the Croatian population. He listed in detail houses that had been burnt, people who had been robbed, people who had been attacked, a number of people who had been killed. There seemed to be quite a lot of consistency about the details of a number of incidents which were mentioned by people on all sides, so clearly there had been a series of incidents which had built up to this. One of the points which he made quite clearly was that when the confrontation initially started very few houses had been burnt, but then in the intervening couple of weeks, I think he said about 40 houses had been burnt, so clearly as people had moved out of their houses, Muslims or whoever, I assume it was Muslims, had come in and burnt the houses, so there was now an issue about people being able to return to their houses. But he was quite clear that at the very beginning there had been relatively little. He talked about four or five houses that had been burnt, when this particular confrontation had actually started. He said that he had initially had some access to Croats being held in Muslim jails. He indicated that there were some prisons to which he did not have access, and he said that at this stage, he did not have access to everybody, so he was again giving a pretty clear and frank exposition of what he thought was going on. It was a very strange experience standing on the steps with him, with his parishioners standing in front of us as he went through the list of issues and then a number of then said, "what about this and that?", talking about friends and relatives who were missing, a very strange experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McLeod, now let us turn our attention to the interviews that are found -- sorry, your interviews with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak. Those are found at annex F in your report. First of all, can you identify how they identified themselves to you and inform the court who they were and the circumstances of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Having been to Cajdras and had the meeting with Father Bozo, we then drove over the hill down into Vitez, and the first meeting which had been set up was with the political and civil authorities -- this is now the Croat authorities in Vitez -- and I met the mayor and Mr. Skopljak, who was introduced to me as the chief of police. I have written his title down as commander of police in Vitez, I understand there may be some discrepancy about his precise title, but my understanding was that he was a senior policeman in Vitez. This meeting took place in the late morning up towards lunch-time on 8th May. It was quite a long meeting, because Mr. Santic seemed to be quite keen to keep talking to me and to explain to me in ever increasing detail his political views. He started off by explaining that I ought to read a novel, I have never actually got my hands on it, but he said if I read this novel this would explain everything to me in some detail. He started off by explaining that the Croats and the Muslims in Vitez actually had no reason to fight, there was no particular justification for them having a conflict, because actually the Croats had all the positions of power in Vitez anyway, so there was no -- his initial position was there was no particular justification for this. He then went on to explain in his view -- the view of events which he wanted to give to me, anyway -- what had happened on 16th April. He explained that in his view the Muslims had attacked and that the Croats in Vitez and the surrounding villages had been taken completely by surprise. They had managed to rally their forces and mount a defence. He also explained that incidentally to this, a number of Muslims in Vitez had been arrested. I cannot remember exactly how many he said, if he gave a number, but he did say that all the Muslims had now been released apart from 13 who were being held in Kaonik Prison for questioning and that now the situation was being stabilised and by the end of this fairly long meeting, he explained in his view what ought to happen next was the international community, so he is saying, "you, the international community, UNPROFOR, need to create a buffer between us and the Muslims in Zenica, as opposed to just allowing the fighting to continue. So it is the international community's obligation to establish a buffer. We can then allow the population to move", and he said quite clearly that he did not see this as being ethnic cleansing, it would be the will of the people that they wanted to move, so all the Muslims would leave Vitez and all the Croats would leave Zenica. Than he concluded by saying, "once we have done this, once there has been this population movement, which would not be ethnic cleansing, his view, then we could proceed to implement the Vance plan, then we could have democracy". But it was a precondition of elections and democracy and all the rest of it that first of all there was a buffer and then a movement of population. During the course of the conversation, again they marked a map for me to explain the tactical situation on the ground. Unfortunately I no longer have that particular map, but yes, it was quite an interesting conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, on the second page of your annex at the bottom of that page, the last sentence, is there an error in your report? Could you read the sentence as it is in the report in English and then inform the court of the correction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is down at the bottom of page F2, where he was talking about the need to provide protection for local civilian population. In the report, what I actually typed up was: "There is a problem with some people who come into people's houses, so Blaskic has ordered his forces not to enter Muslim's houses." When I went through and checked the actual scribbled note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where is it, please, in the French version, could you tell me? So we have managed to find that paragraph. Could you please tell me which is the correct version in French? Could you tell me about the correction? Is it the paragraph starting: "They made some plans to avoid genocide." Is that it, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, could you tell me what is the correct wording now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am just attempting to find my note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will try and help you now. So in the French version, it is marked 626, and now I would really like to know which is the correction that has been made, so it is the one but last paragraph in the French version and the numbers are 573 to 626, and according to Mr. Dubuisson, the paragraph starts: "They really made some plan to avoid genocide, but did obtain the same results and the government insists the military police makes important changes ..." And so on, and saying that the situation in Vitez is going to improve and later on that, "Blaskic ordered his forces not to enter the Muslim houses". Could you please tell me what is the correction that has to be made? "Blaskic ordered his forces not to enter Muslim houses"; is there a correction that has to be made about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The note that I actually wrote was that, "Blaskic has to order his forces not to enter Muslim houses".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have got the correct version. Could you tell me what is the bottom line? What do I have to read here, that Blaskic has to or that he had already ordered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this version in my report, I said that he had, but in the note that I wrote at the time, that he has to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, so the remark should be -- your comment was that Blaskic had to order, still has to do it. That is what I would like to hear, what is your feeling about it in the end, what your conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this was something which he still had to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have understood. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, which means that he had not ordered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, was the note that I wrote at the time of what I was told at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, let us continue now with your examination, in particular, can you now indicate whether or not Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak informed you whether the Muslim population and the Croat populations could live together; in other words, were they advocating polarisation as opposed to reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the view which was being expressed started off fairly moderately but became, in my view, rather extreme, just my opinion, and Mr. Santic was saying that the Muslim population, initially he was saying, "we have no reason to fight them because we have all the positions of power", he said their headquarters was on the rubbish tip, for example, so he was attempting to -- maybe it was, but the impression I had was that he was trying to suggest the Muslim population were lesser. Then, as part of his explanation of why tension had developed, he said that the -- as the war had broken out with the Serbs initially in Bosnia, the Croats had had to form themselves into a defence force, many of the Muslims had left and so I think he was implying that they had run away to go and do business in Zagreb, as opposed to staying to fight. He then made references to the Muslim population having become somewhat extreme in their religious views. He said that he felt that the Muslims were trying to take them back 200 years to the time of the Turks. He said that the wives of leading Muslims within Vitez had started to wear head scarves -- been obliged to wear head scarves. He made reference to the fact they had been driving through the streets speaking with loud speakers and making statements about Allah from the backs of trucks, so he was trying to build a picture of the Muslim population becoming polarised and extreme in their religious views and suggested this was an intolerable situation from the Croats' point of view, and that this was partially seen as a justification for anything which then took place vis-à-vis the Muslim population. I formed the view from the whole feeling of his conversation as he developed his political thoughts over an hour or so that he did not see any particular place for the Muslims within his community, and this was summarised right at the end by saying, "what we need is the international community to set up this buffer zone for us and then we will move the population and then we can be democratic just like you", but he did not see any room for democracy until he had an ethnically pure state, was the impression that I formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, after the population was removed and the Vance-Owen Peace Plan could be implemented, is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. I no longer have a copy of the Vance-Owen Plan as it was at that particular time, but from recollection, what was being suggested I think was that the country would be broken into cantons and that the military and political leadership of each canton would be based on the ethnic composition of the canton at that time, so clearly if one had a mixed canton then the military and political leadership would be mixed, whereas if one had a bias in one direction or the other, the political and military leadership would be biased in favour of Muslim or Serb or Croat, whichever controlled that canton. His aspiration was to achieve a locally balanced, in his view, situation and then immediately to implement the Vance-Owen Plan before the conditions throughout Bosnia were right. That was what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, he also gave you three documents, did he not? Can I direct your attention to those three documents that are attached to the interviews of Messrs Santic and Skopljak. The first document is a document that was signed by Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic and Ivan Santic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It lists five separate points.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and again I am checking to see where the French version is and I have lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we during the recess will put this French version in the correct order, I apologise and it will facilitate your review of this portion of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I would like it to be in proper order, but the documents we are talking about just now, are they annexed to this report? Do they appear in this version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And they come under which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They should follow the interviews of Messrs Santic and Skopljak. There should be three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, I propose since it is 11.15, I give my copy to the Registrar and I hope -- I think we will have a break now and we will resume work in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, bring in the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have reassembled my document, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the deck that was shuffled improperly has now been shuffled in the correct order. I would like to direct your attention first of all, Mr. President, I have taken the liberty of placing a yellow tab at a point in the French translation. Mr. McLeod and I, as we were going through these and putting them into the right order, noticed that there was an incomplete translation, and we would like to direct your attention to it. I have marked II in the French version and that last sentence in II is missing in the French translation. If I could have Mr. McLeod read for your Honour the last sentence in II, then you will be fully informed as to this particular exhibit. Mr. McLeod, could you please read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For my personal benefit, Mr. McLeod, can you tell me that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly sir. In fact it is the last sentence of I leading on after Zenica and it says: "The municipal Civil Defence headquarters is also obliged to provide return of refugees" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Slowly please. "The headquarters of the Civil Defence"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... is also obliged to provide return of refugees from Vardiste to Bilivode".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, when we stopped at the recess, I was directing your attention to three documents that were provided to you by Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak. Can we start with the first document which is a joint statement, it is appendix 1 to annex F? Without spending too much time on this particular document, because this has previously been introduced into evidence, can you just inform the court how you received this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Santic gave me these documents as he was attempting to build his case to explain to me how what he wanted was to have a return to normal life in Vitez, so the first document he gave me was a signed document and he presented this as proof that the Muslim and Croat authorities in Vitez had already decided they wanted to return to a state of normality. If you are already familiar with the document then I will not bother to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. McLeod. Then can you turn to the next document and identify which document it is and inform the court about that particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. So the second document is appendix 2, and this is a draft document which he gave me. He said this was a draft which he had produced which he had sent to his opposite number, the mayor of Zenica, suggesting that they should sign this together and he presented me this document and he also presented me the third document, which was a reply from the mayor of Zenica explaining why this first document which had been drafted in Vitez could not be signed immediately and suggesting some changes. So just to run very briefly through the seven points which had been proposed by Vitez to be signed jointly by Vitez and Zenica, it starts off with a joint declaration that the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in Central Bosnia was not the desire or the will of these two nations, but actually it was all provoked by the Serbs, so it is a Serb plot to destabilise them. He invites the Muslims and the Croats to cease all hostility and immediately to go to peace and that there should be an investigation and punishment of all those who have committed crimes by the regular courts. There is a request, a suggestion that there should be treatment and assistance given to the large number of refugees, a suggestion that the regular police should be used intensively to stop further atrocities being committed, which this declaration suggests are being wrongly attributed to regular forces of the HVO and ABiH. Because there is a complete blockade of the area in terms of supplies getting up from the coast from Split, there is then a joint treaty to the governments, this is the Croat and the Muslim governments, the armies of the ABiH and the HVO, to allow free passage of goods and supplies from the coast up to this area in Central Bosnia. The sixth point says that in order to stabilise the cessation of hostilities, it is a demand from the media, the information media, that in every case they should report only completely confirmed information without personal commentary; in other words, he wants to have complete control over what information is being disseminated to prevent rumours being started or information being incorrectly broadcast, and then finally it is a declaration that as fast as possible, they should implement the Vance-Owen Plan, which as I explained earlier on I think was implementing government and military forces, the control of those to be based on the ethnic make-up of the areas in question. There was also a joint statement by Izetbegovic and Boban of April 25th. Unfortunately I no longer have a copy of that, so I am not sure what the statement was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now can you turn to the reply of the mayor of Zenica to that proposed draft statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. So at the same time I was handed this reply as well as I was handed the unsigned copy of the proposal from Vitez. The mayor of Zenica was basically saying, "yes, certainly we should make a joint statement, but we should make a joint statement which recognises the actual facts as they have occurred as opposed to what has not occurred". So he was suggesting that in practice, there were HVO troops in various villages, Ahmici, Gacice, Veceriska and others, and that the statement, if they were to issue a joint statement, should condemn crimes and should suggest that investigation of crimes should be carried out by a neutral third party as opposed to the local police forces, and that they should work out exactly who was going to be responsible for this, rather than just saying the regular forces should do it; that there should not be a suggestion in the joint declaration that whatever had taken place had been carried out by people who were out of control, but that whatever had taken place had actually been organised by regular forces on both sides. His fifth point I find somewhat confused in terms of exactly what he is suggesting, but basically it is reiterating the fact that there needs to be investigation before there can be reconciliation, I think. The sixth point, again he is coming back to say that he finds it inconceivable that the crimes which were referred to in the joint statement, which he has not signed, were committed by extremists. It ends up by welcoming the initiative and saying that they should do as much as they can to resolve the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McLeod. Mr. McLeod, after the conclusion of your interviews with Messrs Santic and Skopljak, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the office where we had been having that meeting, walked down the stairs into Vitez, walked about 200 yards to the Hotel Vitez, where my next meeting was with then Colonel Blaskic, so what I had been attempting to do was meet the political leadership in Vitez and then the military leadership in Vitez, so I could build up their view of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, could you explain the circumstances of the meeting with Colonel Blaskic and what Colonel Blaskic told you had happened, the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. When I met Colonel Blaskic, General Blaskic now, as I made my general introduction as I had done on each occasion. With him I emphasised the fact I had been in the army, we discussed the fact that he had been in the JNA previously, so we had what at the time felt like a very business-like meeting between two soldiers discussing the military situation, was effectively what it was. My interpreter did the initial part of the meeting and then I think she was having difficulty with the military jargon that we were using, so she stopped and his interpreter took over for the latter, probably two-thirds of the meeting that we had. His interpreter, of course, being more used to the military jargon that was being discussed. Colonel Blaskic struck me as being a fairly straightforward sort of person. It seemed to be a good meeting, his explanation of the tactical situation matched almost exactly the explanation and description that I had had from officers in BritBat. When he marked on the map for me where the forces were and described what he thought the likely outcome of a continuation of the fighting would be, that again matched almost precisely the description I had had from BritBat, so as I suggested the -- he suggested to me that the conflict had only been prevented from getting a lot worse by the intervention of UNPROFOR and he suggested to me that, I cannot remember the exact dates, but soon after 16th April, the Muslim action or reaction, depending on your point of view, but the Muslim attack to cut off Vitez would have been successful if UNPROFOR had not actually been successful in arranging a cease-fire, and this bore out exactly what I had heard earlier from UNPROFOR. So all of those parts of the conversation seemed to make sense. In terms of the precise detail of what had happened on the 16th, you can see exactly what I have written down in terms of the notes that I wrote, but to summarise it, he said that there had been an increasing tension up to the 16th, he said there had been attempts to move Muslim troops on the day preceding this, on 15th April, so tensions had been quite high. On the 16th, he said that he had been woken early in the morning, 5.15, I think, by gunfire and his immediate reaction had been to phone his headquarters and he had spoken to his headquarters and said, "what is going on?", and the duty officer had said that he did not know what was going on, so Blaskic had then said, "well, find out from the local brigade commander what is going on". The brigade headquarters had been phoned and the reply had been the brigade commander is not here, presumably he is asleep in bed, so he suggested they had been completely caught by surprise by what had been going on. He then said that they had rallied their forces as fast as possible and during that morning, they had initially attempted to secure the main government buildings in Vitez and then to carry out the defence of Vitez and the defence of the villages surrounding Vitez, and that eventually the situation had stabilised and the war had been stopped or that localised confrontation had been stopped eventually by the intervention of UNPROFOR arranging a cease-fire. But he was quite clear in his view that if that had not happened then the Muslims would have been successful in cutting the roads on both sides of Vitez and possibly even separating the -- cutting the road between Vitez and Busovaca. At the conclusion of our meeting, he said that as far as he was concerned, it ought to be possible to live together, this is the two parties to live together, but if we were not successful in having an UN buffer of some sort, then he could not actually see much prospect of that and he expected the war to carry on again. Immediately after the meeting, he then had to go off to, I am not sure how -- he had a second meeting and I saw Mr. Santic come down, so Mr. Santic was then joining him in a further meeting to discuss whatever they were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So Mr. McLeod, what he told you in fact was that on the morning of the 16th at 5.15, he was taken completely by surprise, he was awakened by shells and he woke up and it surprised him that there was essentially a conflict going on in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was quite clear that what had happened is the Muslims had launched a co-ordinated attack against a number of positions in Vitez and the outlying villages and that his troops had been caught on the hop and had reacted as well as they could and mounted a defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a couple of portions of your interview with Colonel Blaskic. Did he tell you how many professional soldiers were in the Vitez brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that they had between 300 and 350 professional soldiers and that the rest of the Vitez brigade was made up of reservists and that these were spread through the various villages, where the villages still existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ask Colonel Blaskic to mark a map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I had done in most of my meetings, I gave him a blank photocopied map and a set of coloured pens and invited him to mark on it the tactical situation as he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ask him to mark the identity of particular villages that were occupied by the parties, Muslim, Croat or mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what he did was he marked the map with these highlighter pens with different colours for the different ethnic breakdown or composition of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he mark the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was of interest afterwards when I actually sat down and looked at it to see what he had done, but he missed out the villages of Ahmici, Nadioci and Loncari, and these were the villages which had been the subject of bitter fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And which were not marked by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a comment that Colonel Blaskic made about the events in Busovaca. Could you tell the judges what he said about Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. He described what had happened in Busovaca -- this is, for reference, the third paragraph from the end of this particular annex. He was describing what had happened back in January when the violence had first flared up. He said on 21st January the Busovaca to Kiseljak road was cut and he said that Busovaca had been occupied and ethnically cleansed. He said then, leading on from that, that if the UN did not separate the forces, it was clear there would be further conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that that particular interview with Colonel Blaskic lasted approximately an hour, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably 45 minutes to an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your report accurately reflects then the substance of that interview, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a detailed note of those parts of the interview where I was actually taking notes and I have made a couple of comments about those parts of interview where we were having more a dialogue as opposed to his explanation of events, so fairly shortly thereafter I made a note of what my thoughts were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the interview, what was your opinion as to whether Colonel Blaskic was telling you the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was fairly sure that his description of the tactical situation, because it seemed to match almost exactly what I had been told by UNPROFOR officers, had been accurate. By the time that I had finished speaking to everybody and seen everything that I saw, I cannot actually imagine how, if he was the person that I thought that he was, in other words the military commander of the area, he could have been fast asleep at that point in the morning, because that just did not tally with all the other things which I heard and saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one point of your examination. You have referenced "tactical situation". Could you just tell us what you mean by the term "tactical situation", so the record is perfectly clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The explanation which he gave me of the events following 16th April and his description of the locations of Muslim forces and Croat forces, his view, his opinion that the Muslim forces would have been successful in cutting the various key roads around Vitez, had they not been stopped by UNPROFOR, matched -- it was almost exactly the same explanation as I had been given by UNPROFOR officers, so by the tactical situation, that is what I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, can I direct your attention to part of the interview you had with Colonel Blaskic and that is any reference to outside forces being a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that -- his view was that the Muslims did not want to separate forces, in other words that they wanted to carry on the conflict. He said that there was no clear dividing line between the two sides and that it was a war of neighbours against each other. He said the greatest problem was forces brought in from outside. He said if they were only local forces, then they could have peace. I infer from this that by the forces brought in from outside he is referring to Mujahedin or other Muslim forces brought in on the Muslim side and it was these extremists who had been brought in that were causing the problems. That was my understanding of what he was getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod. Now can we turn our attention to an interview you had with Ramiz Dugalic. Can you tell the judges who he is and the circumstances of that particular interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It is -- "Dugalic" is the pronunciation. Again, on the Muslim side I had been attempting to meet the military command structure so we could get their view of what had happened. With Ambassador Thebault I had already had a meeting with the corps commander of III Corps, who suggested the best person to talk to was one of his deputy commanders, Ramiz Dugalic, I am not sure what rank he had either then or now. He had again set out his view of what the Muslim army, what the Muslim forces thought was the tactical situation, and he described in some detail what he understood had happened or was happening in and around Vitez. I am not quite sure how much detail you would like, but he described various incidents which had taken place with a degree of -- with some detail. Amongst other things, he said that they had caught a couple of Croat prisoners who had been involved in Ahmici. I, of course, said I would be very delighted if I could meet these people and eventually a couple of days later when we came back to this particular issue, he said those two individuals had been exchanged in a prisoner exchange, unofficially, which was rather unfortunate because it would have shed quite a lot of light on what may or may not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, if I can direct your attention to the second page of your report in the English version. Did he also describe units that were part of the HVO and can you tell the judges what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I use the language which comes straight out of the notes which I wrote at the time. He said the HVO had two formations -- it may well have had more than that, but he was talking about two of them. He said they had one legal one which was doing "dirty jobs" as he described it. He said a chap called Darko Kraljevic, now colonel, was in command. He said he had previously been a member of HOS, which was a Croatian military formation. He then showed me a licence which he said had been given to a Muslim to allow the Muslim to leave their home, and I have got a copy of that, there is a copy attached to the report. He then also said that there was another organisation called "Joker" and he said that the leader of this group called Joker was a man called Anto Furundzija, I am sorry if my pronunciation is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, did he make any reference to the truck bomb that had occurred in Vitez itself? Can you tell the judges what he told you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned that there had been a car bomb in Vitez and he said to me that Blaskic had given the order to put the man who drove the bomb into the truck and Darko Kraljevic had carried out the attack. He said his intelligence suggested the HVO wanted to put three tonnes of explosives into the truck, but in the end they only used 700 kilograms. He said the driver had not been a local man but had come back to drive humanitarian aid. They had told him to deliver a message with the truck but had not told him about the explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to note for the record, Mr. President, sorry to interrupt the witness, that the court having made its hearsay rule, the Prosecution is now driving trucks of hearsay through the door that the court has opened. This type of double or even triple hearsay is exactly what should not be the evidence in this case of allegations directly involving our client. I simply wanted to put our further objection on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, this will be in the transcript. Please, Mr. McLeod, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, you indicated that Mr. Dugalic gave you a document which is appendix 1 to annex I. Can you identify that as being the document which was provided to you by Mr. Dugalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a one page, very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am working off the English translation which I have because I can read that and the original is also part of the report. It is titled "certificate for transfer of ownership of property" and the address group at the top of the document is "the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, Department for Defence, Unit Vitezovi, Vitez", and it is dated 24th April 1993. Then the substance of the document is that it: "... confirms that the flat address: M Tita Lamela A5-A9, Ulaz 2, second floor, is given for temporary use to Krizanac Jako by this unit. The former owner of this flat was Ekmescic Faruk." It is signed, "by order, Colonel Darko Kraljevic".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Mr. McLeod. Now let me turn if I can to your next interview. I would like to draw your attention to your interview with the Imam of Busovaca. Could you tell the judges when that interview took place, the circumstances of that interview and the substance of that particular interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 9th May, having by now had two meetings with Croat Catholic priests in the Zenica area, I wanted to try and balance their view with the view of a Muslim religious leader, so I went to Busovaca where I understood that the Imam was still there. I eventually found Enver Hodza in his house, he was just in his back yard, having initially looked at the mosque and he was not there. To start with, he refused to speak to me, but having explained who I was and where I had come from, he eventually decided that yes, he would actually talk to me. So we went into his house and I sat in his front room with him and his wife and his two children, a young girl and a young boy. I went through my usual routine of explaining who I was, where I had come from and what I would like from him. He then explained in some detail his view of what life was like for him and his whatever the equivalent of parishioners is, I suppose, his people in Busovaca. All the time that he was talking, he started off by explaining how there was very little food and so on. His wife was cooking a meal which was then presented to me and Erik Friis-Pedersen who was accompanying me, and we were invited to eat and I said, "I will not eat unless I am joining you in a meal", so I then had to eat a meal with him and Erik while his wife and children watched, which was an extremely uncomfortable experience. At the end of the meeting, as we were just about ready to leave, the Croatian police arrived and came into the house. Presumably they had seen our vehicle parked outside and they wanted to know what we were doing there and wanted to have a conversation there. I suggested that actually since I had finished having my conversation with Enver Hodza but would be delighted to talk to them, we would be delighted to go to the police station, so that is what we did. In terms of the description of what was going on that I was given by this gentleman, he said they were completely isolated, they were quite cut off, they had no communications with Zenica, said that supplies of food were quite short. He said they were unable to leave their houses without permission. He showed me a permit which allowed him to move around. I do not have a copy of that, but I made a note of the details on it in my book. He said they were unable to worship, which was borne out I suppose in part by the fact that the mosque was locked and appeared to be quite deserted. He said that he was, however, allowed to bury the dead and he then went into, I think because it was fresh in his mind, a list of people that he had just buried. As part of his explanation, he explained that a woman had been raped the night before and this was clearly at the forefront of his mind. That particular incident was then carried on, was part of the discussion with the Croatian policeman later on. He said that a number of Muslim families, quite a large number of Muslim families had had to leave their houses and had gone to Zenica. I described the fighting in some of the villages to the north of Busovaca, and he described how the Croats had burnt houses and the Muslims had also burnt houses, so the Muslims had burnt Croat houses and the Croats had burnt Muslim houses. He did not attempt to describe the fact that the Muslims had also been up on the front-line burning people's houses, which is not particularly pleasant. Yes, it was a very strange meeting, sitting with his family in their front room, hearing about events which were a million miles away from these even back in Zagreb, let alone back in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, let me ask you, did he tell you that Muslims younger than 60 years old had to dig trenches for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said amongst other things that they had to go and dig trenches around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he also tell you that Muslims were not allowed to go out of their houses and some had to leave because of HVO violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Referring to the third paragraph from the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, verbatim from my notes, he said they were totally isolated in Busovaca. He said: "There is an information blockade. The Muslims younger than 60 years old have to dig trenches for the HVO. They cannot pray in Busovaca. Muslims are not allowed to go out of their houses and some have had to leave because of HVO violence. He is allowed to bury the dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down, what did he say in respect of the Muslim houses that had been vacated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the context of the meeting which he had had with the president of Busovaca, a man called Zoran Marinic, apparently, and he said he had had a meeting with this gentleman the day before. He had asked for some protection, he had asked for a telephone line so they could have contact outside, in other words back to Zenica. This had been promised, apparently. He then went on to say that all the Muslim houses that were empty had been taken over by Croats and they had all been robbed. Obviously there was a refugee problem, so empty houses were being taken over by Croat refugees who had been moved out of Zenica.
