utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, did he tell you that civilians who had been taken to dig trenches, some of them had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he described a particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am referring to the second page of your report, Mr. McLeod, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that a man by the name of Skandro Kemal had been buried on 24th April, he had been a driver who was arrested between Vitez and Travnik, one of 90 drivers who had been arrested and he had been killed by a sniper digging trenches. He then mentioned another man by the name of Lugonjic Omer who had been buried the day I was there and he said he was also a driver who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me direct your attention to the paragraph three down below that, there is a statement that says: "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots." Is that a quote from the Imam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was in the context, he showed me this pass which he had and I wrote down in my book the details which are then here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This was a pass to pass through from one point in Busovaca municipality to another point, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that it allowed him to move around the town. So the pass was dated 1st May and it was signed by Drsko Grubersic, who was commander of the HVO brigade and Zoran Marinic, President of HVO in Busovaca and Dario Kordic of HDZ and then I wrote in my note, in light of the conversation around this, that Dario Kordic seemed to be the man calling the shots. Clearly that is my jargon as opposed to the jargon of the Imam. I think I had formed the impression at that point that he was clearly the political boss in Busovaca who was directing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges the demeanour of the Imam and his family once the HVO police arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Just about something that I have just heard. I have got a French translation at the end of the paragraph, the reference is 642: "Kordic seems to be the man of the shootings." Is this exactly what you said, Mr. McLeod? In the transcript that I have just had, it says: "Kordic seems to be the man which called the shots." Here in French it says: "Kordic seems to be the man of the shootings." I do not know what is the correct translation? Could somebody give me the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that is a literal or perhaps incorrect translation. It is not what is intended and perhaps Mr. McLeod could explain again his reference to that statement. That was a statement to by McLeod using English jargon and grammar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In French you order to shoot. It seems to be an idiomatic expression. All right, excuse me, I have been surprised but I thank my colleagues for enlightening me. For now I will know that when somebody speaks about the shootings, I will know that that means that person has got the situation under control. Thank you very much, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I had asked you to describe to the judges the demeanour of the Imam and his family upon the arrival of the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as one can possibly imagine, they were rather frightened to have their -- I think it is worth clarifying, from memory I do not think they were HVO police, I think they were civil police, they were wearing blue uniforms as opposed to military uniform. I think they were, as anybody would be, slightly upset to have a couple of policemen come into their living room. They were rather frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not feel particularly comfortable having a second meeting with the Imam and the policemen in his front room so since I had finished my conversation with the Imam anyway, I said to the policemen that I would be delighted to talk to them, but suggested I should come with them back to the police station. So that is exactly what happened, they went back into their police car, we went back into our vehicle, followed them down the road to the police station and immediately afterwards had a meeting with three policemen in the police station in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify the three policemen and the units to which they belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made a note having asked them exactly who they were. I believe I was talking to Nikica Petrovic, who was introduced as the chief of the civil police in Busovaca, Zeljko Lastro of the regional police, I do not know what his title was, but he was described as being of the region police as opposed to any other form of police, and a man called Zoran Vareskovic, who was introduced as deputy chief of the military police. So I had a civil policeman, a military policeman and a member of the regional police, I am not sure what the difference was between the regional police and any of the other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sitting upstairs in the police station in what I assume was a conference room or something like that. They were explaining to me from their point of view what was going on in terms of police matters and they started off by saying that they had problems with a military policeman had just been shot by a sniper, presumably a Muslim sniper. We then rapidly got into discussing the case of the girl who had been raped the night before. I was quite interested and attempted to tease out through the conversation some of the details about what the judicial system was like. I explained to them my previous experience of prosecuting at courts martial and said, "I have some understanding of what might go on", so was attempting to get them to explain the likely sentence for somebody -- they said they had a couple of suspects. I said, "what will happen to these suspects, where will they be tried; if they go to prison, where will they go to prison, how long for?", and they explained what they thought would go on. They said that at that time, the only court which was in operation was the military court in Travnik, and they said that as like as not, the only operating prison was the military prison at Kaonik. They took some pains to distance themselves, or certainly the civilian policeman took plains to distance himself from the prison at Kaonik. He said it was run by Mr. Aleksovski, so he named him as the man who was running it, and said it is a military prison, it is not a civilian prison. We also talked about various other things which were going on, yes. It was a fairly technical meeting with the policemen talking about police issues. Towards the end of the meeting, I said that I had had a meeting with Father Stjepan and Father Bozo, because clearly they were interested to know what was going on on the other side, so I said, "I have had these meetings". I explained the circumstances and the situation of the Croats in Zenica as had been portrayed to me by the two Catholic priests I had met. They said that Bozo, because he brought Croats back to their houses, and the Croats had then been tortured, is what they said, that Bozo, so this is the Catholic priest in Zenica, should be seen as a criminal. He had facilitated the beating up of Croats by bringing them back to their houses in Zenica, and that he was clearly thinking according to his heart and the church by bringing people back to their houses, rather than being in step with the politics, was the note I wrote of the comments they were making.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, when these police officers were talking to you about the HVO prison at Kaonik, did they also tell you that Kaonik Prison was under the jurisdiction of the military court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they said that Zlatko Aleksovski was responsible for the prison, they said it was an HVO prison, not run by the police, and that it was under the jurisdiction of the military court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After those interviews, Mr. McLeod, did you have occasion to go to the Kaonik Prison itself and meet with Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the following day I accompanied Ambassador Thebault and we went to Kaonik and while we were there, we had a long conversation -- yes, a long meeting with Mr. Aleksovski, the details of which are at annex O, so leafing through a little bit. Mr. Aleksovski explained in some detail the difficulties that he had running the prison, what he was doing with the prisoners. He then took me for a tour of the prison block and we then continued the conversation back in his office again. It was quite a bizarre meeting. He discussed the problems that he had, or he explained the problems that he had providing security for prisoners. He said that -- he invited us to understand that because people had lost relatives and then would get drunk, perhaps they would come up and want to beat up a prisoner. As a rhetorical question, he asked whether we would want to shoot someone who had lost a brother to prevent them from beating up a prisoner. His view of that was obviously no, so he explained that we would see none of the jailers in contact with prisoners were carrying weapons, so they would not be put in this difficult position of having to shoot somebody to prevent them from beating somebody up. He talked in some detail about the difficulties of the defence of Busovaca and the fact that there were not enough people to dig trenches and so the fact that prisoners had to go and dig trenches. He said that he knew that this was wrong according to Geneva Conventions but that given the alternative of being overrun by the Muslims, he thought it was justified. He explained that he knew that it was wrong and that one of the ICRC delegates had actually been and explained to him that it was wrong, and that he had gone with her to the local brigade commander in Busovaca where she had remonstrated with the brigade commander. He described an incident where they had been digging trenches and a fire fight had broken out. Once the shooting had stopped they realised two of the prisoners had run away or disappeared, they lost them during the fire fight. All the time that we were having the first part of the conversation, he was attempting to produce a list of prisoners, because he had initially explained that he had a computer with records of who the prisoners were and I said it would be very useful if we could have a copy of this list, so a list was produced and once the list had been printed off, we then went a met a number of people walking -- going into each of the prison cells. In most of the cells there were six or eight people. I had a conversation with some of them. In each of the cells at least one prisoner piped up and asked if they could make a statement about how well they were being treated. In one of the cells, an elderly man asked if he could ask us a question, and I said certainly he could, so through the interpreter, he asked what he was doing there. I, of course, said, "I have no idea what you are doing here". Aleksovski said he knew because he had been speaking to the people who had brought this prisoner in the night before and he had been brought there for his own protection. He had been found wandering around on the contact line, so he was here for his protection. I said, rather quietly, that if I had wanted to protect this person and that was the only reason I had for bringing him to prison, what I would have done was send him to Zenica, say "do not be stupid, walking around in the middle of a front-line, go to Zenica and do not come back again". Aleksovski's reaction to this was to say, "yes, clearly that is right, this is an old man, he can go". Initially he said he could come back with us and then he said in fact he would simply arrange for him to be taken and dropped back at the point where he was picked up. So the man picked up his coat, shook hands with everybody else in the cell and left and there was some toing and froing while they arranged for somebody to take him away. At the end when we left the prison, Aleksovski did not know what the man's name was and I do not know if he was taken back to where he was picked up or taken round the block and back into his cell, but it was a fairly bizarre indication of the degree of control over prisoners which Aleksovski appeared to have, because he appeared to be able to summarily decide that somebody could just leave. Very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod -- so in essence, in fact, Mr. McLeod, he acknowledged the following things; number one that the prison at Kaonik was an HVO prison, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite clearly an HVO prison. During his explanation of what was going on, Mr. Aleksovski had explained that he did not select people to come in, the selection was made by the HVO, that he was actually under the orders of the two brigade commanders in Vitez and Busovaca, so they were responsible for giving him prisoners. We had quite a long debate following the release of this one individual, the apparent release of this one individual, about whether all civilian prisoners should be released or not. We debated the definition of a civilian as opposed to a soldier. Aleksovski put forward the view that a civilian was clearly a civilian, but any man aged between 16 and 60 or thereabouts under these circumstances was a soldier and therefore all the men we had seen were soldiers and therefore by definition could not be released. He eventually said that the decision as to the definition of who was civilians and who was soldiers would have to be taken by the police, as opposed to by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski also acknowledged that sending prisoners out to dig trenches was in violation of the Geneva Conventions, is that correct, that he knew that was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said quite clearly that he knew that it was wrong, but that under the circumstances, he felt he had no choice, because the alternative was not to have the trenches dug and if the trenches were not dug, then the Muslims would have overrun Busovaca and he said, "what would happen to us if that happened?". Given that he explained that he knew it was wrong, he knew that the ICRC had told him it was wrong, I am not sure he knew chapter and verse what the Geneva Convention said in every respect, but he knew that was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He also referenced a specific instance where the ICRC accompanied Aleksovski to Busovaca to talk to the Busovaca brigade commander and inform the Busovaca brigade commander that the use of civilians to dig trenches was in violation of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, did he tell you how many Muslim prisoners had been in the Kaonik camp in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that in January of this year, he had been in the prison when 400 Muslims were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he tell you how many prisoners had been then in the prison at the time you were visiting and the time in and around the time you had visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that at that point there were 79 Muslim prisoners. There had been more. He said on 16th April they had 107 prisoners, on 6th May they had 109 prisoners and on 9th May they also had 109 prisoners. I am not sure that their statistics were completely precise, because they had some difficulty reconciling the list he produced with the people we actually saw, but there or thereabouts I am sure he knew more or less how many he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your visit to the Kaonik camp had been prearranged, had it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You did not just appear at the gates of the of the camp, knock on the door and say, "I would like to see the commander of the prison camp", did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am not sure exactly what the route was by which the message was passed, but we had certainly passed a message, or ECMM had passed a message saying that we would like to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived at the camp, you were given an opportunity to inspect the cells, were you not; some of the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went into one building and we looked into most, if not all of the cells. We saw all the cells that had people in them in that one building. At the time I had the -- I understood that there were more -- a further facility or another building or buildings further down the road. We would have had the opportunity to look at these buildings if we had wanted to, we certainly were not prevented from doing that, but by the end of our visit, we were making some progress around the issue of whether or not civilian prisoners could be released, so we decided we would actually go back to Zenica to try and make progress with that, as opposed to inspecting the rest of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that there were usually six to eight people inside an individual cell: you are talking about six to eight Muslims inside a cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I imagine that the cells were probably designed for one or two people. I would guess they are designed for about that. I cannot remember precisely how many people were in each cell, but it was in that sort of range. There was certainly one cell that we went into off the same corridor which had two Croatian military prisoners. I do not know what they had been charged with, but they were there and there was a stark contrast between them and their circumstances and the circumstances of the other people that we had seen, Muslims we had seen. Possibly they would have put more Croats into a cell if there had been more of them, I do not know, but these two characters had a significant amount of what appeared to be personal possessions. The room was full of bags and rucksacks and bits and pieces which clearly belonged to them, whereas the other people we had seen did not seem to have anything with them and there was certainly a lot more of them in each room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Aleksovski did, in fact, inform you that the civilians that were being kept in the conditions that you have described were being kept there for their own protection, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The basic explanation for having civilians there -- although as I have said, we had this debate about whether they were civilians or soldiers, and they seemed to be either civilians or soldiers depending on how the debate was going, but civilians were there for their protection. It was rather bizarre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the conditions in which you saw the two Croat soldiers, who presumably had been charged with a crime, were considerably better than the conditions in which the Muslims were being kept for their own protection, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the number of people in the cell and the amount of personal possessions which they had, then yes, there was a difference. It may well have been that the Muslims did not have any possessions with them at the time they were brought to the prison, but yes, there was very clearly a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that the Muslim prisoners in the Kaonik Prison that you saw were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the people that I saw were all wearing civilian clothes. There may have been some people wearing a mix, I do not have any particular memory of people wearing mixed uniform and civilian clothes, I am pretty sure I did not see any Muslims wearing uniform. There may have been one or two, but I certainly do not remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to any of those prisoners and identify them as people who had been previously identified to you by the Muslim authorities as being in custody in Kaonik camp, some of the 13 civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I was going into each of the cells, after a while -- rather stupidly, only after a while -- it occurred to me that I ought to make a mark on the list that I had of the people I had actually seen, and so I did eventually realise that I should make a little mark on the list and did so. Certainly there were a couple of people whose names occurred on the list of prisoners which I was given by Mr. Aleksovski which tallied with the list of names I had been given by the mayor of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski also talk to you about the removal of the population from the village of Jelinak? I am referring to page 4 of your report, approximately middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he described to me how in Jelinak, they had gathered all the women and children into one house to protect them from the men who had lost brothers, so presumably this is protecting them from the Croatian men who had lost brothers, and he said: "Then we told them to go to Zenica. They escorted them on foot to the petrol station, then told them to go to Zenica." The petrol station he was referring to was near the Busovaca T junction, so quite close to the prison; also quite close to the no-man's land between the Croats and the Muslims on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he tell you about the village of Jelinak and when it was burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that the BiH now controlled Jelinak, he said the village had been burnt at the very beginning, on the second day of fighting. He said that we were on one side, the Croats were on one side and they, the Muslims, were on the other side. They, the Muslims, had started shelling and the Croats had withdrawn from their positions. Then they, presumably the Muslims had burnt the houses and all of them had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, have you completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to suggest, if you have completed this section on Aleksovski, we could have the break, except if you have more questions on Aleksovski. Of course, let me note that this is the Blaskic trial, not the Aleksovski trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I have a couple more questions and then I will conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Still on Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Related briefly to the Kaonik Prison, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I realise that, you have done well to remind me of that. I know that the Kaonik Prison is part of the indictment. I am seeking to ensure efficiency of the proceedings and I notice that sometimes we repeat things that have already been said in the report. But this is just a comment in passing. I should like us to adjourn now and resume at 3.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume now. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we will continue with the statement by Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and your Honours. Mr. McLeod, before we continue with your testimony, I would just like you to clarify one portion of one of the parts of your report that you referenced earlier this morning, and that is a joint statement that is attached to the materials that were given to you by Mr. Santic and Skopljak and I am referring to appendix 2 to annex F. Specifically, I am referring to the first paragraph in that proposed draft joint statement, and there is a reference on the fourth line down in paragraph 1, the letters "KOS" and I am referring to the sentence that says as follows: "The conflict was provoked by the extreme forces aided by the members of KOS with the purpose of weakening the resistance toward the Serbo-Chetnik aggressor." Can you please tell the judges what you understand to be "KOS", what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I am afraid I do not know exactly what KOS stands for. My understanding in this context is that it might be a Serbian intelligence agency, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. McLeod. Now let me turn to your conclusions in this, based on your experiences on the ground in Central Bosnia, based on your interviews with people from ECMM, from UNPROFOR and from the parties themselves, could you tell the court what conclusions you reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It is worth starting by saying that the report was written at the time for people who were already thoroughly immersed in the situation as it was there and who had access to and were constantly reading a lot of material reporting what was going on, so it was assumed that people understood exactly what the background was, and the conclusions that I wrote were kept deliberately extremely short with all of the other detailed notes of the meeting I had had appended to it. The conclusion that I reached was that on 16th April, the Croatian forces in the Lasva Valley had launched a series of attacks on Muslim positions in Vitez and the villages in the Lasva Valley. At the same time, they had arrested a number of prominent Muslims within Vitez early in the morning of 16th April and I had met some of those people then in Kaonik Prison, I had actually seen them with my own eyes. The most violent attack which they had carried out appeared to be in the village of Ahmici, where as I saw, the majority of the houses which as far as I could tell had been occupied by Muslims had been burnt. I was told that a lot of people had been killed in the village, and I think that was the general understanding at the time, but I certainly saw the village had been razed to the ground and what appeared to have been a fairly serious and a co-ordinated attack. It certainly was not a couple of isolated incidents in the village, it was thoroughly razed. At the same time, there appeared to have been moves to move the Croatian population out of Zenica and there was evidence of this, I was told this, I could see some of the houses that had been burnt after people had moved out and I had the impression that this had been done at least as much at the instigation of the Croats in Vitez in order to justify what they were then doing as a result of fear or intimidation on the part of the Muslims, so it struck me that this movement of Muslim population out of Zenica had been on a different basis, if you like, to that of the Muslim population out of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, let me just correct you, you said movement on the part of the Muslims out of Zenica. Did you mean movement on the part of Croats out of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. It is movement of the Croatian population, Croats living in the Zenica area. Thank you for the correction. By the time that I was in the area in the second week of May, so some three weeks later, it seemed that quite a lot of the Croatian population had been able to return to their houses and there seemed to be evidence -- I was shown things by the Muslim officials but the Croatian priests in Zenica gave the impression that there were steps being taken which while not perfect, they were content that steps were being taken to try and allow Croats to come back to their houses and to allow some semblance of normality to be returned slowly. It was not perfect, but there was progress in that direction. Again, by the time that I got there in the second week of May, in Vitez the Muslim population were concentrated or certainly appeared to be concentrated either in villages which were isolated on the edge of Vitez or in Stari Vitez, old Vitez, in the middle of town, and as far as I could see, there was no freedom of movement, either out of these villages or out of the old sector of town and I went into old Vitez once and there was clearly a degree of fear and people were not able to move out and in, they were not getting supplies of food. I was certainly told about various attacks which were continuing, although while I was actually there there was no artillery fire or sniping against us, probably because we were actually in that part of the town. As far as I could see, and this is based on both what Colonel Blaskic had told me and what UNPROFOR and the ECMM monitors had told me, the Muslim reaction to the attacks on the 16th April had been to try and counterattack, to cut the roads on both sides of Vitez, so as to isolate Vitez and Busovaca, and I think that they had been successful in their counterattacks up to the point when the international community intervened and arranged a cease-fire. I am not quite sure how far things would have got, but I think Colonel Blaskic's appreciation of what might have happened thereafter was probably quite accurate, that the Muslim counterattack would have been quite effective and would have isolated the Croats in Vitez. It struck me, as I sat back at the end of my visit and as I returned back to Zagreb and wrote my conclusions, that on the one hand the Croats that I had met, they left me with the clear impression that what they had been trying to do was to establish a Croatian state in Central Bosnia linked to the Croatian areas further to the west up towards the coast, that what they wanted was to have a largely Croatian or majority Croatian state which they controlled, that they had attempted to force the Muslim population to move out of the area that they wanted to control, that they had been using fairly extreme methods. As a modest Englishman, that is how I would put it, they had been using fairly extreme methods to try and encourage the Muslim population to move. I do not know whether Ahmici was a one-off and it was intended as an example to terrorise people or whether they would have replicated that degree of burning of houses throughout other villages had they been able to. I just do not know, but quite clearly in one particular village they had caused very extreme damage, with the result that the majority of the Muslim population were then either cooped up in a couple of completely surrounded areas or had moved, so by that token, I think they were achieving what they were trying to do. I think they were only prevented from being completely successful by the reaction of the Muslim army, and then intervention of the international community, which stabilised the position in the terms in which I found it some three weeks later, and by the time that I was writing my report, I think it was fair to say -- it would be fair to say that what I would seen in a microcosm in Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica was being played out throughout Central Bosnia and indeed down to Mostar by then, where again, from my point of view, the impression that I formed in light of the information which I could see and all the reporting that I was reading in ECMM was that the same pattern was being replicated, with extreme violence or terror, however you want to describe it, being used to try and move the Muslim population in order to create an one-party state, with only one particular type of people with one religion. So that I think is probably the substance of the conclusions I reached. It is worth noting that the report, the brief one page at the front which I wrote was vetted by headquarters of ECMM, because clearly what I was saying was not to be taken lightly, having been down there, and the deputy head of the mission on the political side, Ole Brix-Andersen, read this and we actually changed the precise detail of some of the elements of what I had written, in fact in order to tone it down. They said, "you could be seen as a young man who has been here, who has witnessed something which is quite terrible and is painting a slightly more extreme view than is necessary", so we actually toned down what I had written a little bit and then they were quite -- by the time we had finished revising it, very rapidly on 15th May, they were content that what we had was as balanced a view as the ECMM could get, and at that point it was published and disseminated as I have described earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod. Mr. President, I would move Prosecutor's Exhibit 242 into evidence and I have concluded then with my direct examination of Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we have ended now the examination-in-chief, is it Mr. Hayman who is going to do the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we have no additional objections to the report other than those previously reserved. Good afternoon. Let me ask you, how many days were you on the ground in the Lasva Valley gathering the data for your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled in on 3rd May and I left on 12th May, so that is nine days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you working all nine days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In that time, you received a briefing from -- one or more briefings from BritBat, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And a briefing from your ECMM colleagues, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Any other briefings from international organisations that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also had conversations with members of the ICRC and also a conversation with a member of UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In addition to the interviews you have recounted, and the documents attached as annexes, did you receive any other documents or have access to any other documents from either of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I think I said earlier on, there were also maps which were marked by people in the other interviews, but unfortunately I have lost those subsequently. But in terms of documents that were given to me, I think I have actually managed to keep everything which I was given, they are included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you received no other military records other than what we have here in Exhibit 242, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pretty sure I managed to hold on to everything and include it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you able to interview any BiH army soldiers or commanders in the Vitez municipality as part of your study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and as I think you can see there is a report of a meeting that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that with a commander in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not talk to any of them. The only other people I could have spoken to I think would have been in Stari Vitez and I did not speak to anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than what you have said in your report, did you gather any additional information concerning the placement or existence of BiH army or Territorial Defence Forces in the Lasva Valley in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you explain exactly what you are after there in terms of, "did I gather"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have said you visited the BiH army command post in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you visited Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a BiH army presence in Stari Vitez when you visited that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certainly -- mm. I am trying to remember seeing people with guns. I think there must have been some people with guns, because otherwise they would have been overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It seems like a reasonable assumption to me. Tell us what you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am attempting to recall precisely what I saw. On the occasion we went into Stari Vitez, there was a meeting taking place and Ambassador Thebault, I think, went to that meeting, but I did not go to the meeting, I sat on top of the vehicle and looked at what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet an individual called Sefkija Dzidic during your visit to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question a moment ago was in addition to those experiences, in the course of your study, did you learn, for example, whether there was an Armija or Territorial Defence position or group in, for example, Donje Veceriska at or about the time it was attacked in mid April 1993? Did you gather any information on that subject, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just work out where Donje Veceriska is and then maybe I can answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Do you have something that would assist you in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a map at the back of my report, so perhaps I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you know where it is, perhaps you could point it out for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the south west of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have better maps if that would be helpful Donje Veceriska is directly west of Vitez. Gacice is south west of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To aid me, I am actually using the map marked by Colonel Blaskic, so I see where Veceriska and Gacice are. If I use the information which he gave me, he marked it as being a mixed village and therefore I would assume that there would have been units from both sides in that village, but I am not sure if that is a suitable answer for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is an assumption, I am glad you have stated it. Can you tell us, as part of your study, did you attempt to gather any more specific information about which of the villages that were the subject of conflict in mid April 1993 had BiH army or Territorial Defence units in them at the time of those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I would like to direct your attention to your interview with Mayor Spahic, which is found in your report, beginning at page A-1, if you would like to have that available for reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you learned in the course of your study --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, which annex? Is it annex A?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe it is beginning on page A-1, Besim Spahic, mayor of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The French version does not have the page numbers at the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You learned in this interview or in another that some 2,000 Bosnian Croats had fled the Zenica municipality during the conflict in mid April 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did someone tell you that that was due principally to propaganda disseminated by Bosnian Croats themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the impression that I was given, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I probably formed that impression based on my meetings and conversations with people in Zenica, a combination of the Muslim officials I spoke to and then also the priest that I spoke to, as well as what I was told by members of ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that any such propaganda emanated from then Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was being precise about exactly who was disseminating that information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest that any such propaganda emanated from the operative zone level of the HVO command in Central Bosnia; that is Colonel Blaskic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was saying precisely where the propaganda was being generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you interview any of the 2,000 displaced persons to determine from them why they fled the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn from your interviews whether during this period of time in the middle of April 1993, whether the Zenica municipality, was it a safe or was it an unsafe locale, generally speaking, for Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the period leading up to the middle of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From the 16th on, beginning on 15th or 16th April and in the following days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was probably relatively unsafe in comparison with the way it had been immediately before that and I would evidence that by the fact that people were taking steps to make it safe again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described one meeting with Father Stjepan and a meeting with Father Bozo. I would like to ask you about apparently a second meeting you had with Father Stjepan, which is recounted, and again I apologise, Mr. President, the best way for me to find pages is to use the alpha-numeric designation at the bottom of the page. This is on page E-2, and that is the second page in the English version of your notes or write-up of your meeting with Father Bozo of Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see what you are referring to, it is the second and third paragraphs on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in connection with your meetings on this day, did you also meet with Father Stjepan and did he present you with a list of problems and difficulties that the Croat population in the Zenica municipality had been facing or was facing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did those include the statement by Father Stjepan that: "We are now in danger." And: "MOS come at night to their homes", referring to the homes of Bosnian Croats or HVO soldiers, "and take them." Did he make that statement to you, in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that if we turn to appendix 1 to that annex, then you can see the English translation and the original typed report as I was given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he also tell you, two paragraphs further down in your statement of your meeting with Father Bozo that: "They shoot pigs and steal cows and they take food day and [something]. Criminals take everything and destroy everything." Was that also a statement he made to you, Father Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he say a couple of paragraphs further down in your report that to date, and that would have been as of 8th May, 65 or 70 homes have been burnt; did he make that representation to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said only one house was burnt during the conflict and now, so presumably that is in the intervening three weeks, 65 or 70 houses have been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the aftermath of 16th April 1993, some 65 or 70 homes of Bosnian Croats in the Zenica municipality have been burned; was that your understanding of what you were being told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He summed up two paragraphs later by stating: "Increasingly there is no security so people leave." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Later on, over on the next page, he recited various statistics of the number of dead, houses burned and robbed, including a total of 12 civilians killed in the conflict, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said earlier I believe that Father Stjepan, he was a moderate who advocated ethnic reconciliation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your interview with Mayor Spahic, did he tell you in substance that he was doing everything he could to prevent violence and attacks against Croats in the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think when I took what he said in context with what other people were saying as well, that seemed to be what they were trying to do. I think as I said earlier on, the circumstances were fairly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were very difficult, so despite the best efforts of the authorities in the Zenica municipality, some 70 Bosnian Croat houses had been burned, 12 civilians had been killed and there was a general state of lawlessness and lack of security, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what one can deduce by taking this at face value, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is a fair inference, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please give us an audible answer, that would help for purposes of the transcript. Now Mayor Spahic also showed you a decree, did he not, which he issued on 18th April 1993 and which is found in your report at page A1-1. For purposes of the French version, Mr. President, that is appendix 1 following the statement of Besim Spahic titled, "orders for the return of refugees to Zenica". In that decree or statement, directing your attention to I, did the mayor call for the establishment of joint checkpoints and joint patrols to include both Armija and HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn from your study that at the time this was issued -- and I apologise, this is dated April 17th 1993, not 18th -- did you learn from your study that at this time in fact the BiH army had attacked the HVO in Zenica and there was ongoing armed confrontation between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case and so what they were trying to do was to stop that. My recollection is not perfect, but I think that there was an area of Zenica where there was still a fight going on, or had been going on, but I think there were other areas which were returning to calm and they were probably, this is my inference, suggesting that in those areas where there was not a fight going on, they ought to have joint patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Although at this time, would you agree in those areas where the Armija and the HVO was not in actual conflict, that was because the HVO had been captured and they were locked up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if all of them had been locked up, but yes, certainly a number of them had been, as evidenced by the priest that I spoke to, who talked about the people in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Turning to the next page, I think it is a different decree, although there is no real title, it is title, "Conclusions", I and II, and it is dated April 18th 1993. Let me first direct your attention to that. Have you found it? In the bottom numbering in the English it is A1-2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In this document, Mayor Spahic called, in I, for the respective headquarters of the warring parties to "immediately give orders for unconditional cease-fire"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D76, Mr. Registrar, if D76 could be retrieved to be provided to the witness. While that is being retrieved, let me ask you, in the course of conducting your study, did you learn that in fact Colonel Blaskic issued an order on this day, 18th April 1993, calling for a cease-fire on the part of the HVO? If you would provide it to the witness, please? Specifically I would direct you to paragraph 1 of that order. Did you learn that in the course of your study, that Colonel Blaskic ordered a cease-fire on the date Mayor Spahic called for it, 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but it sounds as if they were working quite closely in co-operation and looking at the addresses on this, I imagine that this was the product of one of the Joint Commissions which was being run at that time by Colonel Stewart and Ambassador Thebault, so the fact we have the two things at the same time is probably on both sides the result of the same meeting, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the BiH army command issued a similar order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we put the exhibit on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. President. My mental lapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Because this dialogue between the Defence and the witness is something that the judges would like to participate in. I think this is an exhibit that you have already offered? Yes, I think I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. There is a French written translation available. I was calling the witness's attention to paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I still do not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, if we could zoom in on the order, please? If we could enlarge the middle portion of the text of the order, please. Thank you. Calling the witness's attention, I was, Mr. President, to paragraph 1 and I will read it so we can obtain a sight translation: "I command 1. All the subordinate HVO units are to stop immediately all combat actions against the units of the ABiH." I was posing a follow-up question and that is: did you learn in the course of your study whether the BiH army command issued a similar call or order for a cease-fire on 18th April 1993, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the English translation of the document dated 18th April, you do not see the address list, but if you turn to the original, which is a few pages on, it is A1-6, then down at the bottom I think we can see the address list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So a copy of this document, the decree, if you will, of 18th April 1993, we can tell from this copy which is part of your report that it went to the HVO in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so it goes to III Corps of the ABiH -- shall I put this on the projector as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please. You are directing your attention to the lower left-hand corner which is the distribution list in Serbo-Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think what we can see here is -- this is the document signed by the president, by the mayor of Zenica, it is going to III Corps of the ABiH and then is also going to the HVO in Zenica, so he is disseminating the same order in the area that he controls and I assume that the original document you would have shown me would have been disseminated on the Vitez side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This document, would you agree, this is a conclusion of the mayor that the respective headquarters are requested to give an order for a cease-fire; that is the contents of Mayor Spahic's document in I, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would infer that what was happening was that the political control was saying, "stop fighting", and then I imagine, but I do not have a copy of, an order which would then have been disseminated from III Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You would expect that III Corps would have issued a similar cease-fire order on 18th April 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume so. If, as I imagine, there was a tripartite meeting, a Joint Commission, they would have agreed they were going to do it and what we see on both sides is that information being disseminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They would have done so if they were working with the political forces and the HVO to achieve a cease-fire in the same way that the HVO command was, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I would assume, although I do not have that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to your interview with Father Stjepan which begins on page B-1 of the English version and that is annex B, Mr. President. In paragraph 4 of this statement, it appears Father Stjepan described a process of action/reaction that he stated was occurring within Central Bosnia and he described, for example, a family expelled from Vitez causes a reaction here, meaning in Zenica. Did you hear this concept described by others, such as when the Imam of Busovaca described threats being made to Muslim residents of Busovaca by Croat refugees from surrounding villages who had been expelled and were in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that despite the breakdown in communications, in practice people could communicate and there were a number of examples both in terms of what was happening to people in their houses and also what was happening to prisoners to suggest yes, there was a degree of tit for tat, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the next page of your report, again this same interview with Father Stjepan, did he complain of a problem of discrimination against Bosnian Croats in Zenica in that, for example, former steelworkers who were of Croatian ethnicity, or at least those who had been said to have joined the HVO, were not given food rations which were at the time a substitute for salary or pension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the justification -- not justification, the explanation which he gave was that, or that he had been given was that these people were now in prison, and because they were in prison, they were not working and therefore not getting their food ration, but the substance is exactly that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Because others similarly situated, fighting, otherwise not employed, they were getting a food ration as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct you to the next interview you document in your report, the head of ICRC Zenica, I will not use his name in case there is an issue, but you met with the head of ICRC Zenica on 7th May 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him what access ICRC had to Bosnian Croat prisoners who were being held in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in light of my previous experience working in the humanitarian section, I was aware of the need to be in close co-operation with the ICRC and so one of the things that I did, as you can see fairly early I wanted to go and meet them and say, "we are taking various steps as best we can" and to make sure we did not tread on their toes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you how many prisons there were in Zenica holding Bosnian Croat prisoners at the time, 7th May 1993? Paragraph 2 I would direct your attention to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He alluded to three prisons, one of which they had access to and two of which they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you name them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. He said they had access to the main prison, I do not know what the main prison was called other than being the main prison, and then he said not to the MUP, which I assume is the police prison, or the music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The MUP is the Ministry of State Security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am not sure if that is exactly what the initials stand for, but that is what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The music school, did you understand that was the headquarters of 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know it was the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade, but I did understand it was a facility controlled by that entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me direct your attention to your interview with Father Bozo, which is in Appendix E of your report. I take it when you spoke to him, was this the meeting at which you were on the steps of a church or a building, and there were a number of parishioners surrounding you and the Father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I said earlier on, we started off in his house, we then went for a tour to a village at the top of the hill, and then came back to the church, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he describe, as set forth in paragraph 2 of your report, that parishioners in his area, the Cajdras area, left their homes after they were subjected to pressure and houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so my note is that he said that 80 per cent of people stayed in their homes and after that there was high pressure and burning of houses and threats, so after that, all of them ran away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then two paragraphs later, does he describe an incident of looting in which the looters had military uniforms, and when the military police from the III Corps of the Armija arrived, they let the robbers escape but they took into custody an Australian TV crew that was trying to film these events; did he relate that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the state, if there was a state of anxiety and agitation among the parishioners around you at the time; what was their state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were extremely concerned to know what was going on, they were extremely concerned to know what had happened to individual members of their families, and they wanted to know what was going to happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you view their concerns as real?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention forward in your report to appendix F, your interview with Santic and Skopljak. At the bottom of page 1 of your report, there appears to be an allusion, I assume by Mr. Santic, to information of an impending attack on 15th April 1993. Can you elaborate on that for us? What was the information that Mr. Santic gave you in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we have here is precisely what I wrote down, there may have been some more detail which I missed. What he was saying was that on 15th April, so the day before everything broke down, that there was a rumour of an attack from Zenica to Vitez, so people were agitated. I think that would be how I would characterise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn in your study of any other events on 15th April 1993 that might have lent credence to that type of a report, such as any attacks on HVO commanders, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that at the time the Armija was certainly capable of launching a significant attack on Vitez from Zenica, with the forces available to it in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so and I think that one can see from what happened a few days later; we will not say it is an attack or a counterattack, but certainly they proved themselves capable of making ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In that such a military action took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of this statement, did Mr. Santic also tell you that because there was an explosives factory in Vitez, I believe he said "every tenth man has too much explosives", or explosives in his private custody; did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you determine from your study or investigation whether in fact there was an explosives factory in the immediate vicinity of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me direct your attention to the bottom of page F-1 in the English report. This is the statement of Mr. Santic which you have advised is inconsistent with your notes, namely the statement concerning whether Blaskic had ordered his forces not to enter Muslim homes or has to order, has to make such an order. Do you find that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bottom of F-2, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you prepared your report initially from your notes, did you base it solely on your notes or did you also use your actual recollection of these interviews and what was said at the interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, I just sat and typed the hand-written notes straight up as you see here, which is why the grammar is less than perfect, and then also as you can see, I interspersed with comments, bits based on what I could remember, as opposed to that which I had written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After you typed it up, your notes, did you read over it to determine whether your notes were consistent with your actual recollection of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which is why I was able then to add comments. I started off by typing the basic text from my notebook, then ran through it and added in the comments and interspersed comment so people could tell the difference between a note and my own thoughts, recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The comments aside, when you were writing up the actual statements of the interviews, did you also call upon your recollection of the interviews in checking, if you will, the accuracy of what you were writing, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly did in places where what I wrote tailed off or was incomplete. In this particular case, and I could show you the note in the original if you are interested, but I think the original is fairly clear, I was working quite fast and made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As you sit here today, do you recall what was said on this subject in the interview, or are you totally dependent on your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think for precision I would go back to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection as you sit here on what was said in the interview on this issue yourself? It was four years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not be able to say with any degree of certainty, that specific element, whether it was in one tense or the other tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D43 could be obtained, Mr. President, and placed before the witness. The ELMO could assist, I think, all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, do you have D43?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the text, particularly the preamble and paragraph 1, that would be helpful. Thank you. This is an order dated 22nd April 1993 which in part reads, from then Colonel Blaskic, which reads: "In order to prevent incidents in which houses and other commercial facilities are set on fire and looted, I hereby issue the following order. "1. I strictly prohibit the torching of houses and other commercial facilities and looting in the zone of responsibility of the command of the Central Bosnia operation zone controlled by HVO units." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question is: does that refresh your recollection as to any discussion you may have had with Mr. Santic concerning the fact that such an order had been issued by Colonel Blaskic concerning the protection of Muslim homes and businesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if one takes into context the preceding sentences before the precise sentence where we think we have a potential misunderstanding or inaccuracy, and if I read the preceding sentence: "The government insists that local military police in Vitez must be larger and it was done yesterday. I think that the situation in Vitez will be better from day-to-day." I think in that context, clearly the situation was still not perfect, so clearly this is an order dated before my meeting with him. I can quite easily imagine a situation where the order was given, the order is quite clear and explicit, the order may either not have been carried out properly or there may have been a subsequent reason why things had broken down again, but at the time I was having this conversation with the mayor, I think what he was telling me was, "we still need to make things better."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What kind of an order did you understand Mr. Santic to be suggesting; that is, do you think an order could have been issued stating, "no soldier shall enter a Muslim home for any purposes, including if the home is a source of fire", that is rifle or sniper fire or something like that; is that the kind of order that you thought Mr. Santic was actually referring to, or did it not make sense to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In context, I think he was referring to soldiers going into people's houses and beating them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To attack them or loot them or burn their house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As opposed to military action because they thought somebody was shooting at them. In the context I think there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to make a small break between the question and answer, please, for the benefit of the interpreters. Could you please answer the previous question? Could you repeat the previous question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, my question was: did you understand in essence what Mr. Santic was referring to, was suggesting that an order would be appropriate that would prevent HVO soldiers from attacking Muslims in their homes or looting their homes or seeking to burn or damage their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding in the context of my notes was that he was saying that HVO soldiers should be told not to go into Muslim houses to beat them up or loot them, as opposed to an order to prevent HVO soldiers from firing on a Muslim house where they were being fired on, from which they were being fired on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what caused you to compare your report with your notes on this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can imagine before coming here, I was refreshing my memory and going through and checking and this is a detail where there was a difference, and I think that it is reasonable to say that as far as one can, let us be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you were reading your notes to further refresh your recollection before testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nearly five years ago, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention forward, although it is actually appendix D, and that is your report of interview with Mr., or General Hadzihasanovic, appendix D to your report. His position at the time was commander of the Armija III Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You met with him and had an interview with him, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there during a very brief meeting which was actually being run by Ambassador Thebault at which Ambassador Thebault effectively had a brief de marche and one element of that was, "that this chap McLeod is here from Zagreb, he needs to speak to somebody, could you recommend the appropriate person for him to speak to?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it in the course of that encounter, there was a substantive discussion on a certain number of points and you have memorialised those in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you conclude from your interview with General Hadzihasanovic that he had been truthful and candid with you in all respects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that it was a very brief meeting, as far as I could tell he was telling us what he thought. I have very little on which to base the judgement as to whether he was telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Among the things that he told you, he told you that although he was the commander of the III Corps, he had no knowledge of any prison in the MUP or state security or any prison in the music school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you find that credible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think looking at the notes, there is a discrepancy, if I may be allowed to correct myself, between what he has got there and then the fact that access to the music school was not a probable, but he would have to make a phone call first. In practice I think he did have knowledge of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could one not read -- excuse me, did you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I actually noted this meeting in much detail, so I think what we have here is me working from memory as opposed to working from a verbatim account, which is why it is such a short note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that General Hadzihasanovic said to you in this meeting that he did not know there was a music school, I am asking whether his statement that he had no knowledge that there was a prison or a location where Croats were being held prisoner in the music school, whether you found that credible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that if one looks down to the next line where he is talking about access to the music school, I am quite confident from what I wrote there that what he was talking about was access to a prison there as opposed to simply being able to go into the school. There is an inconsistency between what I wrote in the second paragraph and what I wrote in the third paragraph, for which I apologise, but this was five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If he said that he had no knowledge of a prison in the music school, would it not be natural for him to say, "but you can go look, access is no problem". Would that not be entirely consistent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic also said that he had to go slowly because he wanted to have the 7th Muslim Brigade under control rather than not; did he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then did he go on to say, "the Mujahedin are not under control and there are many elements who are not controlled"; did he make those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not clear by the time that I finished exactly what the chain of command was with the 7th Muslim Brigade, so I did not really have a view on that. Clearly this entity existed, the 7th Muslim Brigade. Precisely what the chain of command was, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me direct your attention to appendix I, your interview with Commander Dugalic. You have written in your report that Ramiz Dugalic was the deputy commander of the III Corps Armija; do you know what his responsibilities were in the III Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was an intelligence officer or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the top of the second page in the English version, he told you that an HVO formation doing the dirty work was Darko Kraljevic's unit, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He added that Mr. Kraljevic was an illicit drug user?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And in connection with that discussion, he gave you a document which is attached to your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you will turn to that document which is I1-1 in the report, you will see that it is signed and the title of the individual signing the ratification is "Colonel Darko Kraljevic". Did you also understand from your study that Tihomir Blaskic at the time was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn as a result of your study what the relationship was of Colonel Blaskic to Colonel Kraljevic within the HVO chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From your knowledge of military structures, is it possible to have two colonels on the same terrain in the same chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the -- to complicate things slightly, in the British army you can have two people both called a colonel and one is a full colonel and one is a lieutenant colonel. I am not sure if there was any difference in rank with apparently the same sounding title and I can imagine having two people of the same rank. It certainly exists in the UK right now in the home command, where you have two people of the same rank one being superior to the other, which does not help anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say, "within the home command", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been out of the army for five years, nearly six years now, but I understand right now in the UK the way the army is structured, there are people of the same rank, one of whom is in charge of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that be within a central command location, or would that also be true out in the field during wartime, for example, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure.
